lessons.title: Why Hybrid Identity Exists
lessons.chapterTitle: Hybrid Identity: Connecting On-Prem AD to the Cloud

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free Microsoft Entra ID tenant (no cost, via a Microsoft 365 developer subscription or a plain Entra free tier) and record its initial default domain (e.g. yourcompany.onmicrosoft.com). Then, using Caldwell Logistics' real numbers from this course (roughly 600 employees, 60+ security groups, an ERP system and file servers tied to a 12-year-old on-prem AD forest, caldwell.local), write a one-paragraph memo to Caldwell's CIO explaining why abandoning that AD forest for a cloud-only identity on day one would break more than it would fix, and why hybrid identity is the only workable path.
slots.deliverable: A real Entra ID tenant with its default domain name recorded, plus a written CIO memo citing Caldwell Logistics' actual on-prem footprint to argue against a cloud-only cutover.

lessons.title: Microsoft Entra Connect and Directory Synchronization
lessons.chapterTitle: Hybrid Identity: Connecting On-Prem AD to the Cloud

slots.practicalActivity: In your Entra tenant from last session, open the Microsoft Entra Connect / Connect Health blade (even with nothing synced yet) to see exactly where sync status would appear, then write out, in your own words, what Get-ADSyncScheduler, Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta, and Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Initial each actually do. Work through Caldwell Logistics' 9:05 a.m. new-hire example by hand: given a 30-minute default cycle whose last run was at 9:00 a.m., name the exact clock time the new hire's account will appear in Entra ID.
slots.deliverable: Notes from the real Entra Connect/Connect Health blade in your tenant, written explanations of the three ADSync cmdlets, and the exact worked clock-time answer for Caldwell's new-hire sync example.

lessons.title: Federation vs. Password Hash Sync
lessons.chapterTitle: Hybrid Identity: Connecting On-Prem AD to the Cloud

slots.practicalActivity: Write a one-page comparison memo recommending PHS, Federation (AD FS), or Pass-Through Authentication for two fictional organizations: (1) Caldwell Logistics — a two-person IT team with no existing AD FS investment and no rule barring password hashes from leaving the network; (2) a hospital network under a compliance rule that passwords must never leave the corporate network. Justify each recommendation using the lesson's real tradeoffs — setup/maintenance cost and what happens to cloud sign-in if on-prem infrastructure goes down — not just by naming the option that sounds more secure.
slots.deliverable: A written two-case comparison memo recommending PHS for Caldwell Logistics and Federation for the regulated hospital network, each justified by the lesson's real operational tradeoffs.

lessons.title: AWS IAM Identity Center and External Identity Providers
lessons.chapterTitle: Hybrid Identity: Connecting On-Prem AD to the Cloud

slots.practicalActivity: Create a free-tier AWS account (or use an existing one), enable AWS Organizations, turn on IAM Identity Center, and create one real permission set, recording its exact managed-policy contents. Then, continuing the Caldwell Logistics scenario, design the full SAML federation setup: Entra ID as the external identity provider, one Entra ID group (AWS-Platform-Engineers) mapped to that permission set on two named AWS accounts (Networking, Security), and write the one sentence explaining exactly what happens to the engineer's AWS access the moment they're removed from that one Entra ID group.
slots.deliverable: A real IAM Identity Center permission set in a free-tier AWS account, plus a written SAML federation design naming the exact Entra ID group, AWS accounts, and permission set for a Caldwell Logistics platform engineer.

lessons.title: Never Trust, Always Verify: What Zero Trust Actually Means

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short comparison table contrasting how Caldwell Logistics' developer signing in from the office vs. from a hotel room would be treated under the castle-and-moat model versus Zero Trust. Then map each of the three Zero Trust tenets (verify explicitly, least privilege, assume breach) to one specific, named Entra ID control you'd actually configure for that developer's account — not a vague description, the real feature name.
slots.deliverable: A written two-row comparison table (office vs. hotel sign-in, old model vs. Zero Trust) plus three named Entra ID controls mapped one-to-one to the three Zero Trust tenets.

lessons.title: Microsegmentation Applied to Cloud Networks

slots.practicalActivity: In a free-tier Azure subscription, create (or reuse) a resource group with a VNet containing a web subnet and an app subnet, create two NSGs, and write rules on each that allow only web-subnet-to-app-subnet traffic on port 443, denying everything else by default. Then add an Application Security Group grouping VMs by role (web/app) instead of by subnet IP range, exactly as the lesson describes, and write one sentence explaining why the ASG-based rule keeps working even if a VM's IP address changes.
slots.deliverable: Two real Azure NSGs enforcing a deny-by-default, port-443-only rule between a web and app subnet, plus a working Application Security Group grouping VMs by role instead of IP range.

lessons.title: Identity as the New Perimeter

slots.practicalActivity: In your Entra ID tenant, enable MFA (Security Defaults or a per-user policy) on a test account. Then write a short incident-style note imagining Caldwell Logistics' cloud HR SaaS app has no firewall or VPN of its own at all: walk through exactly what single thing stands between an outsider and employee payroll data, and name the specific control you just configured that stops a stolen password alone from being enough.
slots.deliverable: A test account with MFA actually enabled in a real Entra tenant, plus a written incident-style walkthrough naming identity as the sole gate and MFA as the specific control defeating a stolen password.

lessons.title: Continuous Verification and Conditional Access Policies

slots.practicalActivity: If your tenant has Conditional Access available (Entra ID P1 trial), build one real policy requiring MFA for a test group. Then write out, step by step, what happens to an already-signed-in session if that user's device compliance status changes mid-session: does the policy wait for a fresh login, or does it catch the change on the user's very next access attempt? If no P1 trial is available, write out the policy's exact conditions and controls as if configuring it for real.
slots.deliverable: A real (or fully specified) Conditional Access policy requiring MFA for a test group, plus a written step-by-step explanation of how it re-evaluates a session whose device compliance changes mid-stream.

lessons.title: Encryption at Rest: How Cloud Providers Actually Do It
lessons.chapterTitle: Cloud Encryption: At Rest and In Transit

slots.practicalActivity: Create a free-tier Azure Storage account and a free-tier AWS S3 bucket, and confirm in each platform's own portal that encryption at rest is already enabled by default with zero configuration from you. Then write one paragraph explaining precisely why a stolen, valid access key to that storage account would still let an attacker read the data in plain form, despite encryption at rest being on.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Storage account and S3 bucket with encryption-at-rest settings confirmed on by default in each portal, plus a written explanation of why a stolen access key defeats encryption at rest.

lessons.title: Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS Concepts
lessons.chapterTitle: Cloud Encryption: At Rest and In Transit

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real Azure Key Vault and a real AWS KMS key (the AWS free tier covers the first 20,000 KMS requests a month). Inspect each service's access-policy / IAM key-policy screen, then write a short comparison of what each service does and doesn't store — Key Vault's keys, secrets, and certificates in one vault versus KMS's keys-only scope, with secrets and certificates split out to separate AWS services.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Key Vault and a real AWS KMS key, each with its access-control screen inspected, plus a written comparison of their scope differences.

lessons.title: Customer-Managed vs. Platform-Managed Keys
lessons.chapterTitle: Cloud Encryption: At Rest and In Transit

slots.practicalActivity: In the Key Vault from last session, generate a real RSA key, then, if your storage account's tier supports it, switch its encryption source from Microsoft-managed to that customer-managed key and confirm the switch in the portal. Write one paragraph explaining crypto-shredding — specifically, what happens to every piece of data that key protects the moment you deliberately delete it, and why that's a legitimate data-destruction technique rather than a mistake to avoid.
slots.deliverable: A real customer-managed key created in Key Vault (wired to a storage account's encryption source where the tier allows it), plus a written explanation of crypto-shredding as a deliberate data-destruction technique.

lessons.title: TLS and Encryption in Transit for Cloud Services
lessons.chapterTitle: Cloud Encryption: At Rest and In Transit

slots.practicalActivity: In your Azure Storage account, confirm Secure transfer required is enabled, then attempt (and watch fail) a plain HTTP request against it. Separately, write the exact S3 bucket policy statement that denies any request where aws:SecureTransport is false, and note the minimum TLS version each platform currently enforces by default.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Storage account with Secure transfer required confirmed and a failed plain-HTTP request as proof, plus a written S3 bucket policy statement enforcing aws:SecureTransport and the enforced minimum TLS version for each platform.

lessons.title: Why You Never Hardcode a Secret

slots.practicalActivity: In a throwaway local git repo, commit a file containing a fake-but-realistic connection string, then delete the line in a follow-up commit and run git log -p (or git show against the earlier commit) to prove the "deleted" secret is still fully recoverable from history. Write one paragraph naming the two other places, beyond the repo itself, a hardcoded secret can leak to.
slots.deliverable: A local git repo where a fake secret was committed and then "deleted," with git log -p output proving it's still recoverable from an earlier commit, plus a written list of the two other leak points.

lessons.title: Azure Key Vault Secrets in Practice

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real secret in your Key Vault (a fake prod-orders-db-connection value), update it once, and confirm Key Vault auto-versions it. If you have an Azure Function App or VM available, enable its system-assigned Managed Identity, grant it a scoped Key Vault Secrets User role on just that one secret's vault, and write the DefaultAzureCredential retrieval path the app would use with no credential of its own stored anywhere.
slots.deliverable: A real, versioned Key Vault secret, a Managed Identity granted a scoped read role on the vault, and the written retrieval code path proving no credential is stored in the app itself.

lessons.title: AWS Secrets Manager and Parameter Store

slots.practicalActivity: Create a real secret in AWS Secrets Manager (a fake database credential as JSON key/value pairs) and a real SecureString parameter in Systems Manager Parameter Store for a fake internal hostname. Compare each service's cost and rotation screens, then write one paragraph justifying why a production RDS password belongs in Secrets Manager while the hostname belongs in Parameter Store, citing the lesson's real cost and rotation differences.
slots.deliverable: A real AWS Secrets Manager secret and a real Parameter Store SecureString parameter, plus a written justification citing the real cost and rotation tradeoff between the two.

lessons.title: Secret Rotation and Access Policies

slots.practicalActivity: On the Secrets Manager secret from last session, configure (or fully document, if no RDS instance is available) an automatic rotation schedule, then work out, with real day counts, the exact "window of usefulness" a leaked password would have rotated every 30 days versus never rotated at all. Write the least-privilege access grant for that one secret (one identity, one secret, deny everything else by default) and contrast it with the "whole team gets read access" anti-pattern the lesson warns against.
slots.deliverable: A rotation schedule configured (or fully specified) on a real secret, a written window-of-usefulness comparison with real day counts, and a written least-privilege access grant contrasted against a broad-team-access anti-pattern.

lessons.title: What CSPM Actually Does
Common Cloud Misconfigurations CSPM Catches

slots.practicalActivity: In a free-tier Azure or AWS account, deliberately create one of the five real misconfiguration patterns from this lesson pair in a throwaway resource (e.g. flip an Azure Storage account's Allow Blob public access to enabled, or open a security group to 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22) just long enough to see it as a genuine finding, then immediately revert it. Write a five-row table naming each of the five common misconfigurations (public storage, an open 0.0.0.0/0 admin port, wildcard IAM Action/Resource, disabled encryption at rest, unenforced MFA on a privileged account) and, for each, the exact baseline rule a CSPM tool compares it against.
slots.deliverable: A written five-row misconfiguration table naming each pattern and its baseline rule, with at least one pattern actually created and reverted in a real free-tier account as a hands-on check.

lessons.title: Microsoft Defender for Cloud and AWS Security Hub Concepts
Compliance Scoring and Remediation Workflows

slots.practicalActivity: Enable Microsoft Defender for Cloud's free foundational CSPM tier on your Azure subscription (no cost) and record the real Secure Score it reports. In an AWS account, enable Security Hub and note which underlying services (GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, IAM Access Analyzer) it's aggregating findings from. Then work the lesson's compliance-score math by hand — an environment passing 312 of 340 CIS Benchmark checks — and write one paragraph explaining why that percentage isn't directly comparable to a separate 95% PCI DSS score from the same environment.
slots.deliverable: A real Secure Score reading from Defender for Cloud and/or a real Security Hub findings aggregation view, plus the hand-computed 312/340 compliance-score percentage and a written explanation of why scores from different benchmarks aren't comparable.

lessons.title: Site-to-Site VPN Fundamentals

slots.practicalActivity: In a free-tier Azure subscription, create a VPN Gateway's required GatewaySubnet and a Local Network Gateway resource describing a fake on-prem public IP and address range (stop before provisioning the full VPN Gateway itself, since that can run beyond free-tier cost and take 30-45 minutes). Then write out, naming the exact two gateway resources per platform (Azure: VPN Gateway + Local Network Gateway; AWS: Virtual Private Gateway + Customer Gateway), why a colleague's claim "we don't need site-to-site VPN, we already have VNet peering" is wrong for connecting an on-prem office.
slots.deliverable: A real Local Network Gateway resource definition in Azure, plus a written explanation of why VNet peering can't substitute for a site-to-site VPN connecting an on-prem network.

lessons.title: Azure ExpressRoute and AWS Direct Connect

slots.practicalActivity: Without provisioning an actual circuit (real cost, weeks of lead time), draw out the real path for each platform: your on-prem network, a connectivity provider's cross-connect, the ExpressRoute location or Direct Connect location, a dedicated port (1/10/100 Gbps), and finally Azure or AWS — naming Azure's Private Peering vs. Microsoft Peering and AWS's Direct Connect Gateway for multi-region reach. Write one paragraph answering why ExpressRoute needs no IPsec configuration the way a site-to-site VPN does, and name one real workload type where that distinction is a hard compliance requirement.
slots.deliverable: A written, correctly-ordered diagram of the ExpressRoute/Direct Connect physical path for both platforms, plus a written explanation of why no IPsec is needed and a named real-world compliance-driven use case.

lessons.title: When VPN Is Enough and When You Need a Dedicated Circuit

slots.practicalActivity: Using the lesson's own two named scenarios, write a recommendation memo for a regional clinic chain sending nightly non-urgent backup data with no compliance rule, and a payment processor running a primary, always-on PCI-regulated transaction link. Name VPN for one and a dedicated circuit for the other, explicitly explaining why the compliance detail outweighs raw traffic volume in the payment processor's case, then describe the "VPN as automatic failover behind a primary ExpressRoute/Direct Connect circuit" pattern in one paragraph.
slots.deliverable: A written two-scenario recommendation memo (clinic to VPN, payment processor to dedicated circuit) explicitly reasoning from compliance over traffic volume, plus a written description of the VPN-as-failover pattern.

lessons.title: Point-to-Site VPN for Remote Users

slots.practicalActivity: If you have access to an Azure VPN Gateway in point-to-site configuration (or a trial/sandbox one), install the Azure VPN Client and note the two real authentication options (certificate-based or Entra ID sign-in). If none is available, fully document the exact configuration you'd use for a Caldwell Logistics remote engineer who needs direct access to a private internal database with no public endpoint. Write one paragraph explaining the old workaround (routing through a full office site-to-site VPN first, then out to the cloud) and exactly what point-to-site skips.
slots.deliverable: A documented (or real) point-to-site VPN client configuration naming its authentication method, plus a written explanation of the old site-to-site-first workaround P2S eliminates.

lessons.title: The Shared Responsibility Model, Revisited for Compliance

slots.practicalActivity: Locate a real Azure ISO 27001 reference on the Microsoft Service Trust Portal, or a real AWS SOC 2 report reference in AWS Artifact, and identify exactly which layer it attests to (the "OF" layer: datacenter, hypervisor, network backbone). Write one paragraph explaining, using Caldwell Logistics as the example, why that certificate alone doesn't make Caldwell's own storage-account public-access setting or logging configuration compliant, naming the term for the legitimate shortcut an auditor still accepts for the infrastructure layer.
slots.deliverable: A located real AWS Artifact or Microsoft Service Trust Portal reference, plus a written explanation distinguishing the provider's certified "OF" layer from Caldwell Logistics' own unaudited "IN" layer, naming compliance inheritance.

lessons.title: SOC 2 and ISO 27001 Applied to Cloud Environments

slots.practicalActivity: Write a SOC 2 scoping memo for Caldwell Logistics choosing which of the five Trust Services Criteria apply — Security is mandatory; justify in one sentence each whether Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, and Privacy apply to a logistics company's order-tracking app. Then map four real controls you've already built hands-on earlier in this course (MFA, Key Vault encryption, a least-privilege access policy, a retained log entry) to the specific SOC 2 criterion or ISO 27001 Annex A control area each one serves as evidence for.
slots.deliverable: A written SOC 2 criteria-scoping memo for Caldwell Logistics with justified in/out decisions for all five criteria, plus a four-row table mapping real controls built earlier in this course to the specific area each serves as evidence for.

lessons.title: Compliance Frameworks in Azure and AWS Tooling

slots.practicalActivity: If your Azure subscription has access, open Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager (or Azure Policy's built-in regulatory compliance initiatives) and assign or review one framework (e.g. NIST CSF or ISO 27001:2013), recording the real score and at least 2 named gap items. If you have an AWS account, start an AWS Audit Manager assessment against a prebuilt framework (e.g. CIS Benchmarks) and note which of your real AWS Config/CloudTrail data it's already pulling evidence from. Write one paragraph tracing exactly how an Azure Policy regulatory compliance initiative's results flow into the Defender for Cloud dashboard from Chapter 5.
slots.deliverable: A real compliance-framework assessment result with at least 2 named gap items recorded, plus a written trace of how Azure Policy initiative results reach the Defender for Cloud compliance dashboard.

lessons.title: Preparing for a Cloud Security Audit

slots.practicalActivity: Build a real, mini audit-evidence folder from this course's own hands-on work, one item per the lesson's three evidence categories: export or screenshot one configuration item (an IAM policy JSON or RBAC role assignment), one access-log entry (a real Azure Activity Log or AWS CloudTrail event you can actually pull), and name one policy document Caldwell Logistics would need written (its security policy or incident response plan). Write one paragraph explaining why "stale access" is one of the most common real audit findings even at organizations with otherwise strong technical controls.
slots.deliverable: A real three-item evidence folder (one configuration export, one access-log entry, one named policy document) mapped to the lesson's three evidence categories, plus a written explanation of why stale access keeps showing up as a finding.

lessons.title: Lab: Setting Up Hybrid Identity Sync
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Securing a Hybrid Cloud Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Walk through Caldwell Logistics' own Entra Connect decision in writing, as if you were its two-person infrastructure team: name the exact installation choice (Custom, not Express) and why, name the sign-in method chosen (Password Hash Sync) and the specific operational reason federation was rejected. Write the three real verification commands in order (Get-ADSyncScheduler, Start-ADSyncSyncCycle -PolicyType Delta, Get-ADSyncConnectorRunStatus) and what each one would have caught if Caldwell had skipped it, then describe exactly what you'd check in a newly synced user's sign-in logs to confirm a Conditional Access policy actually reached that account.
slots.deliverable: A written walkthrough of Caldwell Logistics' Entra Connect setup naming the installation choice, the PHS-over-federation decision with its real reason, the three verification commands with what each catches, and the specific sign-in-log check that proves Conditional Access actually reached the new account.

lessons.title: Lab: Encrypting Data and Managing Secrets End to End
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Securing a Hybrid Cloud Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce Caldwell Logistics' lab for real in a free-tier Azure subscription: create a Key Vault with soft-delete and purge protection enabled, generate an RSA customer-managed key in it, create a Storage account, grant its managed identity the Key Vault Crypto Service Encryption User role, and switch its encryption source to that key with the real az storage account update command. Separately, store a fake database connection string as a Key Vault secret with az keyvault secret set, then write one paragraph explaining exactly why Key Vault can auto-rotate the key on a schedule but can only set an expiration notification on the connection-string secret.
slots.deliverable: A real Azure Key Vault with purge protection, a real customer-managed RSA key wired to a Storage account's encryption source via a managed-identity role grant, a real Key Vault secret holding a fake connection string, and a written explanation of why keys and secrets rotate differently.

lessons.title: Case Study: Remediating a CSPM Finding
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Securing a Hybrid Cloud Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the investigation, not just the fix: in a free-tier Azure subscription, create a Storage account and a container, deliberately enable AllowBlobPublicAccess and set the container's public-access level to Blob, then run the real az storage container list command from the lesson, filtering for public containers, to confirm what's actually exposed. Remediate with both commands from the lesson (the account-level az storage account update --allow-blob-public-access false and the container-level az storage container set-permission), then write one paragraph explaining why running only the account-level command, while sufficient to close the exposure, would still leave a dangling container-level setting an auditor could flag later.
slots.deliverable: A real Storage account and container deliberately exposed then confirmed exposed via the real az storage container list query, remediated with both the account-level and container-level commands, plus a written explanation of why both commands were run.

lessons.title: Chapter Capstone: Identity, Networking & Security Review
lessons.chapterTitle: Capstone: Securing a Hybrid Cloud Environment

slots.practicalActivity: Write the full course-closing synthesis in your own words: walk through Caldwell Logistics' story in order (sync accounts, verify Conditional Access reaches them, encrypt the storage account with a CMK, move the connection string into Key Vault, catch and remediate the public-access finding, tie it all to SOC 2/ISO 27001 evidence) and, for each of the course's 7 content chapters, name the one real artifact you personally built hands-on in this course that chapter's concept produced. End by answering the lesson's own closing question: which Lesson 29 decision only paid off because of something built in a later lesson, and which lesson made it matter.
slots.deliverable: A written course-closing synthesis walking through Caldwell Logistics' full story in order, naming one real hands-on artifact you personally built per chapter, plus a direct written answer to the lesson's own cross-chapter closing question.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can design and defend a real hybrid identity and Zero Trust architecture across Azure and AWS — explaining and choosing between password hash sync, federation, and pass-through authentication, bridging on-prem AD into both Entra ID and AWS IAM Identity Center, and justifying least-privilege Conditional Access and microsegmented NSG/security-group rules — and can actually operate the controls underneath it: provisioning a customer-managed key in Key Vault or KMS, moving a hardcoded secret into Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager with a real managed-identity retrieval path, reading a real Microsoft Defender for Cloud Secure Score or AWS Security Hub findings view, choosing correctly between a site-to-site VPN, ExpressRoute/Direct Connect, and point-to-site VPN for a given workload, and tracing a SOC 2 or ISO 27001 control back to the real Azure/AWS configuration that serves as its evidence. They've personally reproduced Caldwell Logistics' own capstone build end to end — wiring a storage account to a customer-managed key, retrieving a secret through a managed identity instead of a config file, and investigating, remediating, and re-confirming a real public-access CSPM finding — so the whole chain from identity sync to a closed, verified audit finding is something they've actually done, not just read about.
